description: I’m Abhiram, a cybersecurity enthusiast from Hyderabad. Team CipherPulse is building secure health monitoring software for astronauts: simulated vitals, AI anomaly detection, and encrypted offline-first storage with tamper detection. Expect a live demo, not just slides. I bring cybersecurity and threat modeling skills. Looking for: a frontend/UI dev, a data/ML person, a backend dev, and a designer or storyteller. Beginners welcome. Message me to join!
summary: CipherPulse is a secure, real-time astronaut health monitoring console. Wearable sensors stream vital signs: heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, breathing and radiation. Each reading is digitally signed and checked for forgery and replay, then encrypted and stored in a tamper-evident chain. An AI layer combines safe limits, personal baselines, machine learning, trend forecasting and mission-phase awareness. AI agents then explain every alert in plain language, with suggested actions. The system keeps recording when contact with Earth is lost and syncs when it returns. Users explore a realistic 3D astronaut with an X-ray view, an orbit view, and a narrated beginner tour. Clicking an organ opens related research from NASA’s open science data repository (OSDR), NASA’s DONKI space-weather events, NASA images and technical reports, each labelled by source. Live vitals in the demo are simulated and clearly marked as such. CipherPulse gives mission control early, explainable warnings while protecting sensitive medical data when links are slow or unreliable, which matters for long-duration missions far from Earth.
details:
CipherPulse is a secure, real-time health monitoring console for astronauts on long missions. Wearable sensors stream five vital signs every second: heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, breathing rate and radiation. Each reading is digitally signed (Ed25519). The gateway rejects forged, replayed or physically impossible packets, then encrypts valid ones (AES-256-GCM) and stores them in a hash-linked chain, so any edit or deletion is detected. An AI layer then analyses every reading: mission-phase-aware safe limits, each astronaut’s own baseline, an Isolation Forest anomaly model, pattern recognition and trend forecasting. A LangGraph agent explains each alert in plain language with suggested actions, and a 0 to 100 health index summarises each astronaut. If contact with Earth is lost, wearables keep recording and sync in order when the link returns. A NASA tab connects to NASA OSDR studies, DONKI space-weather events, the NASA Image Library, NTRS reports and the Human Research Roadmap. Every item is labelled by source.

Benefits and intended impact
Crews and flight surgeons get earlier, explainable warnings, and can trust that the data has not been forged or altered, even when links are slow or unreliable. The aim is to support human decision-making, not replace it or diagnose anyone. The same approach could help other remote settings, such as polar stations or disaster response.

Creativity
A realistic 3D astronaut carries a live heart monitor on its chest. In X-ray view the heart beats and the lungs breathe at the astronaut’s real data rates, and clicking an organ opens related NASA research. An orbit view shows the radio link to ground control: the beam turns red when the link is cut, and queued packets collect around the station. Built-in attack buttons (forge, replay, tamper with the vault) let anyone watch the security work. A narrated 17-chapter guided tour drives the real system to explain it to beginners.

Tools and technologies
Python, FastAPI, WebSockets, SQLite, scikit-learn, NumPy, pandas, LangGraph, optional Claude, Groq and Gemini models, MCP and A2A endpoints, JavaScript, Three.js with bloom effects, HTML and CSS, the browser speech APIs, and pytest (27 tests). It runs on an ordinary Windows, Mac or Linux computer. No special hardware is needed, because the wearables are simulated. We used Claude (an AI assistant) to help write and test code.

Factors we considered
Delayed and unreliable space communication, privacy and integrity of medical data, explainability, avoiding false alarms through mission phases, and honesty about data. No public source of live astronaut vital signs exists, so the demo vitals are simulated and labelled SIMULATED_DEMO. NASA data is kept separate under its own labels. Space-weather events are never presented as an astronaut’s radiation dose. It is a prototype, not a medical device.
